tool.name: ShadowPolygons
tool.summary: Creates concentric ring buffers around the (dissolved) polygons of a feature class, with a Transparency attribute that fades outward, so the rings render as a soft black cartographic shadow that makes the source features stand out.
tool.usage:
The tool dissolves the input feature class into a single source polygon and builds a series of ring buffers around it. If the input layer has selected polygons, only those are dissolved and used; otherwise every polygon in the feature class is dissolved into the source.
Each ring is stored as its own polygon with a Transparency value that increases from the innermost ring outward. When the rings are drawn in solid black with the fill transparency varying by the Transparency field, the innermost ring is the most opaque and each successive ring is more transparent, creating a shadow that fades away from the source features. The dissolved source polygon is included in the output with a Transparency of 100 (fully transparent), so it never obscures the real features drawn on top of it. A layer file symbolized this way is created next to the output feature class.
You choose the number of rings and the size of the outermost ring. The outer size can be given as a proportion of the width or the height of the source polygon's extent, or as an absolute distance in meters, kilometers, feet, or miles. The rings are spaced evenly between the source and that outer distance.
If the source feature class uses a geographic coordinate system, the rings are buffered geodesically so they are correctly shaped on the ground. The tool honors the Output Coordinate System environment (the finished output is projected into it).
Because the rings are purely for cartographic effect, the source polygon is generalized slightly before buffering, so the rings are approximate and lightweight rather than an exact analytical buffer.

dialogReference.para: The polygon feature class or layer to build the shadow around. If the layer has a selection, only the selected polygons are dissolved into the source; otherwise all polygons are dissolved together.

The output polygon feature class of ring buffers. It contains one record per ring plus the dissolved source polygon, with Buffer_Size and Transparency fields. A matching layer file is written beside it.
How many ring buffers to create around the source polygon. The default is 10. Each ring is one step of the outermost size, spaced evenly from the source outward.

The distance from the source polygon to the outer edge of the outermost ring, interpreted using the Size units setting. When the units are a proportion of the extent, this is a fraction (for example, 0.25 means one quarter of the extent width or height).
How to interpret the outermost buffer size. Choose a proportion of the source extent's width or height, or an absolute distance in meters, kilometers, feet, or miles.

The transparency, in percent, of the innermost ring (the darkest part of the shadow). The default is 50. Each successive ring outward is more transparent, up to nearly 100 percent at the outermost ring. Must be at least 0 and less than 100.

scriptExample.title: Create Shadow Polygons example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Build a 10-ring shadow whose outer edge is one quarter of the source extent width, with the innermost ring at 50 percent transparency.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\Tools\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") arcpy.jenness.ShadowPolygons( in_features=r"C:\Project\Study.gdb\StudyArea", out_fc=r"C:\Project\Study.gdb\StudyArea_Shadow", num_rings=10, size_value=0.25, size_units="Proportion of extent width", min_transparency=50)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Creates fading concentric ring buffers around a polygon as a soft cartographic shadow.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Creates concentric ring buffers around the dissolved polygons of a feature class, with a Transparency attribute that increases outward. Drawn in black with transparency varied by that field, the rings form a soft shadow that makes the source features stand out. Selected polygons are used if the input layer has a selection, otherwise all polygons; geographic inputs are buffered geodesically. The dissolved source polygon is included with Transparency 100. The rings are approximate (the source is generalized first) and intended for cartographic effect, not analysis.
